questions.q: If $z = f(x, y)$ where $x = g(t)$ and $y = h(t)$, what is $\frac{dz}{dt}$?
questions.answer: By the multivariable chain rule, rates of change sum across all intermediate paths: $\frac{dz}{dt} = \frac{\partial z}{\partial x}\frac{dx}{dt} + \frac{\partial z}{\partial y}\frac{dy}{dt}$.

questions.q: Given $z = x^2 y$, $x = t^3$, and $y = t^2$, find $\frac{dz}{dt}$ at $t = 1$.
If $z = f(x, y)$ with $x = r\cos\theta$ and $y = r\sin\theta$, what is $\frac{\partial z}{\partial r}$?
questions.answer: $\frac{\partial z}{\partial r} = \frac{\partial z}{\partial x}\frac{\partial x}{\partial r} + \frac{\partial z}{\partial y}\frac{\partial y}{\partial r} = \frac{\partial z}{\partial x}\cos\theta + \frac{\partial z}{\partial y}\sin\theta$.

questions.q: What is the gradient vector $\nabla f(x, y)$ of a scalar function $f(x, y)$?
questions.answer: The gradient of a multivariable function is the vector consisting of its first-order partial derivatives: $\nabla f = [f_x, f_y]$.

questions.q: Compute the gradient $\nabla f(2, -1)$ for $f(x, y) = 3x^2 y + 2y^2$.
What is the geometric relationship between the gradient $\nabla f(x_0, y_0)$ and the level curve $f(x, y) = c$ passing through $(x_0, y_0)$?
choices: $\nabla f(x_0, y_0)$ is perpendicular (orthogonal) to the tangent line of the level curve
$\nabla f(x_0, y_0)$ is parallel to the tangent line
$\nabla f(x_0, y_0)$ has zero dot product with the normal vector
$\nabla f(x_0, y_0)$ points along the curve
questions.answer: The gradient vector at any point is always perpendicular to the level curve (or level surface) passing through that point.

questions.q: What is the formula for the directional derivative $D_{\mathbf{u}} f$ in the direction of a unit vector $\mathbf{u}$?
questions.answer: The rate of change of $f$ in the direction of unit vector $\mathbf{u}$ is the dot product of the gradient with the unit vector: $D_{\mathbf{u}} f = \nabla f \cdot \mathbf{u}$.

questions.q: Why must $\mathbf{u}$ be normalized to a unit vector before computing $D_{\mathbf{u}} f = \nabla f \cdot \mathbf{u}$?
choices: To ensure the derivative measures rate of change per unit of geometric distance
Because dot products cannot be computed with non-unit vectors
questions.answer: Normalizing $\mathbf{u}$ ensures that the directional derivative accurately reflects the instantaneous rate of change per unit distance along that direction.

sections.heading: Section 4: Direction of Maximum Increase & Steepest Ascent

questions.q: In which direction does a differentiable function $f$ increase most rapidly at a point?
choices: In the direction of the gradient vector $\nabla f$
In the direction opposite to $\nabla f$ (i.e. $-\nabla f$)
Along the tangent to the level curve
questions.answer: Since $D_{\mathbf{u}} f = \|\nabla f\| \cos\theta$, the maximum rate occurs when $\cos\theta = 1$ ($\theta = 0$), pointing in the exact direction of $\nabla f$.

questions.q: In which direction is the rate of change of $f$ equal to zero?
choices: In any direction tangent to the level curve (orthogonal to $\nabla f$)
Nowhere, a differentiable function always changes
questions.answer: When $\mathbf{u}$ is orthogonal to $\nabla f$, $\cos\theta = 0$, so $D_{\mathbf{u}} f = 0$, which occurs along tangent directions to level curves.
